meta.title: How AI Text Watermarking Works (Interactive Demo) | Orange Labs
meta.description: Claude now watermarks its text using Google DeepMind's SynthID-Text. Run the same tournament sampling mechanism yourself, word by word, and see how detection actually works.
meta.ogImageAlt: Orange Labs interactive demo: how AI text watermarking works, word by word

hero.headline: Watch an AI watermark get written, one word at a time
hero.sub: Claude now watermarks its text using Google DeepMind's SynthID-Text. There are no hidden characters to strip. The watermark is the word choice itself. Here's the mechanism, running live on whatever you type.

sixtySecond.heading: If you only read four lines, read these

items.text: Watermarking is centuries old. Two kinds: visible (logos on stock photos) and invisible (only software can see it).
Anthropic rolled out the invisible kind for text in August 2026, using SynthID-Text.
It works on word choice, not hidden characters. Copy-pasting it anywhere changes nothing.
Only Anthropic can currently check for it. A public detection API is forthcoming.

simulator.heading: The tournament sampling simulator
simulator.intro: Type or paste anything below. Every word with a plausible alternative competes in a small tournament, seeded by your key and the words right before it. Change the key and watch every outcome change.
simulator.disclaimer: Simulation. This runs the same mechanism on a demo key, not Anthropic's key. It cannot detect real Claude text.
simulator.mechanismNote: The real SynthID-Text samples candidates from the model's full probability distribution over its vocabulary and runs a multi-layer knockout tournament. This demo swaps in a small, fixed dictionary of 2 to 5 alternatives per word, so you can see the mechanism run in a browser.

samples.label: A factual paragraph
samples.text: SynthID-Text was created by Google DeepMind and published in Nature in 2024. Anthropic uses it to watermark Claude's text.

samples.label: A code snippet
samples.text: function add(a, b) { return a + b; }

detector.heading: Now check your own work
detector.intro: The detector looks at the same words your run just chose and asks: were these picked because of the key, or would any writer have picked them anyway?
detector.wrongKeyLabel: Run the detector with the wrong key
detector.wrongKeyNote: Same text, different key. If the score collapses to about 0.5, that's the whole point: the key is what makes the watermark readable, nothing else about the text does.

stressTest.heading: Try to break it yourself
stressTest.intro: Run the four transforms below on your watermarked output and watch the confidence readout before and after, side by side.

tests.label: Copy-paste it
tests.caption: No hidden characters. Nothing to strip.

tests.label: Shorten to one sentence
tests.caption: Small samples score poorly. Your caption probably won't register.

tests.label: Light edit (swap ~10% of words)
tests.caption: Light editing probably won't remove it.

tests.label: Full rewrite
tests.caption: A complete rewrite where every word is replaced will.

meaning.heading: What this means for your team
items: Factual and low-entropy writing carries less watermark. There are fewer word choices to work with.
When Claude only edits your draft, the watermark lives only in the words Claude changed.
A watermark means "Claude touched this," not "no human wrote this."
No watermark proves nothing at all. Absence of a signal isn't evidence of anything.

context.heading: Why now, and what's still open

items.heading: Why now
items.body: The EU AI Act's Code of Practice has roughly 190 signatories, so most model providers are building their own version of this.

items.heading: Images and files work differently
items.body: Pictures and documents get C2PA content credentials in their metadata instead of a text watermark. That's a weaker guarantee, since metadata is easy to strip.

items.heading: The quality cost was tiny
items.body: Google measured a 0.01% difference in thumbs-up rate across roughly 20 million Gemini responses when SynthID-Text was turned on, a gap small enough to be statistically insignificant.

goDeeper.heading: Go deeper
goDeeper.note: A production implementation ships in Hugging Face Transformers v4.46.0 and later.

items.q: Can you remove a Claude watermark by copy-pasting the text?
items.a: No. There are no hidden characters, invisible Unicode, or metadata involved. The watermark is the specific words the model chose, and copying or pasting text doesn't change a single word, so it doesn't touch the signal at all.

items.q: How long does the text need to be for detection to work?
items.a: Neither Anthropic nor Google publishes a minimum word count, but the pattern is consistent: longer passages give the detector more watermarked words to average over, which raises confidence. Very short snippets, like a one-line caption, generally won't carry enough signal to register.

Barely, and that's expected. Code has exact syntax with very few interchangeable word choices, so there's little room to apply a word-choice watermark. Comments within code, and translations of text, carry a full watermark since they involve normal language choices.

items.q: Can it tell who wrote something, or which specific person or chat it came from?
items.a: No. The watermark carries no identifying information. It cannot be traced to a user, an organization, or a specific conversation, and it can't confirm human authorship or identify other AI systems either.

items.q: Does watermarking hurt Claude's output quality?
items.a: Google's own measurement, across roughly 20 million Gemini responses using the same SynthID-Text approach, found a 0.01% difference in thumbs-up rate, small enough to be statistically insignificant. There's no added cost, no added tokens, and no meaningful speed impact.

items.q: If Claude only edits my draft instead of writing it, does the watermark still apply?
items.a: Only to the words Claude actually changed. If Claude lightly edits a paragraph you wrote, the watermark lives in those specific edits, which may be too few words to register with any confidence.
